questions.prompt: What is the average-case time complexity of a hash table lookup?
questions.explanation: With a good hash function and low load factor, lookups are amortized O(1). Worst case (many collisions) degrades to O(n).

questions.prompt: What is the average time complexity of accessing an element in a dynamic array by index?
questions.explanation: Dynamic arrays support constant-time random access via index.

questions.prompt: Which data structure uses FIFO (First In, First Out) ordering?
questions.explanation: Queues process elements in the order they were enqueued.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of lookup in a hash table with many collisions?
questions.explanation: With poor hashing or many collisions, lookup degrades to linear scan.

questions.prompt: In a balanced binary search tree, what is the time complexity of search?
questions.explanation: A balanced BST halves the search space at each level, giving O(log n) search.

questions.prompt: Which data structure uses LIFO (Last In, First Out) ordering?
questions.explanation: Stacks push and pop from the same end, so the most recently added element is removed first.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of inserting at the head of a singly linked list (given a pointer to the head)?
questions.explanation: Head insertion only requires updating a few pointers, regardless of list size.

questions.prompt: What property does a min-heap maintain?
options: Every parent is smaller than or equal to its children
Every parent is larger than or equal to its children
The tree is always perfectly balanced
All leaves are at the same depth
questions.explanation: In a min-heap, the smallest element is at the root and each parent is ≤ its children — ideal for priority queues.

questions.prompt: For a sparse graph with few edges, which representation is typically more space-efficient?
options: Edge list with full vertex pairs
questions.explanation: Adjacency lists store only existing edges, while an adjacency matrix uses O(V²) space regardless of edge count.

questions.prompt: When is a hash set preferred over a sorted array for lookups?
options: When you need average O(1) membership checks on unsorted data
When memory must be minimized at all costs
When duplicate values must be preserved in order
questions.explanation: Hash sets provide fast average-case contains checks without maintaining sorted order.

questions.prompt: Why is a linked list often preferred over a dynamic array for frequent insertions at the front?
options: Linked lists have O(1) random access
Linked lists avoid shifting all existing elements on each front insert
Linked lists always use less memory than arrays
Linked lists guarantee cache-friendly memory layout
questions.explanation: Array front inserts require shifting O(n) elements; linked list head inserts are O(1).

questions.prompt: Why are B-trees commonly used in database indexes?
options: They guarantee O(1) lookup in all cases
They stay balanced and minimize disk reads with high branching factor
They store data only in leaf nodes with no internal keys
They are simpler to implement than hash tables
questions.explanation: B-trees are shallow and disk-friendly, reducing I/O compared to binary tree structures.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array?
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the search space each step, giving O(log n).

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm has a best-case time complexity of O(n)?
questions.explanation: Insertion sort runs in O(n) when the input is already nearly sorted.

questions.prompt: What does the Master Theorem help analyze?
questions.explanation: The Master Theorem provides closed-form solutions for common recurrences.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm design paradigm breaks a problem into independent subproblems, solves them recursively, and combines results?
questions.explanation: Divide and conquer splits the problem, solves subproblems independently, and merges results.

questions.prompt: What is the average-case time complexity of Quick Sort?
questions.explanation: Quick Sort averages O(n log n) with good pivot selection, though worst case is O(n²).

questions.prompt: What is the time and auxiliary space complexity of Merge Sort?
options: O(n log n) time, O(1) space
O(n log n) time, O(n) space
questions.explanation: Merge Sort always runs in O(n log n) but requires O(n) extra space for merging.

questions.prompt: Which traversal uses a queue and explores neighbors level by level?
questions.explanation: BFS processes nodes in order of increasing distance from the start, using a FIFO queue.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between greedy algorithms and dynamic programming?
options: Greedy always uses recursion; DP never does
Greedy makes locally optimal choices without revisiting; DP solves overlapping subproblems with stored results
Greedy is only for graphs; DP is only for arrays
Greedy guarantees optimal solutions; DP does not
questions.explanation: Greedy commits to the best immediate choice; DP builds optimal solutions by caching subproblem answers.

questions.prompt: What problem does Dijkstra's algorithm solve?
options: Finding shortest paths from a source in a graph with non-negative edge weights
Detecting cycles in a directed graph
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm computes shortest paths from a single source when edge weights are non-negative.

questions.prompt: The two-pointer technique is commonly used on:
options: Unsorted arrays to find pairs meeting a condition in linear time
questions.explanation: Two pointers on a sorted (or appropriately structured) array can solve many pair/sum problems in O(n).

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a base case in recursion?
options: To stop the recursion and prevent infinite self-calls
To allocate heap memory for the call stack
To convert the algorithm from top-down to bottom-up
questions.explanation: Without a base case, recursive calls never terminate.

questions.prompt: A sorting algorithm is 'stable' if:
options: It always runs in O(n log n) time
It preserves the relative order of equal elements
questions.explanation: Stability matters when sorting records by multiple keys — equal primary keys keep their original order.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a process and a thread?
options: Processes share memory; threads do not
Threads share a process's memory space; processes do not
Threads require more memory than processes
questions.explanation: Threads within the same process share address space; processes have isolated memory.

questions.prompt: Which scheduling algorithm can cause starvation?
questions.explanation: Low-priority processes may never run if higher-priority work keeps arriving.

questions.prompt: What does virtual memory allow an OS to do?
options: Run programs faster than physical RAM allows
Give each process the illusion of a large, private address space
Eliminate the need for a hard drive
Share CPU time equally among processes
questions.explanation: Virtual memory maps process addresses to physical RAM or disk, giving each process its own address space.

questions.prompt: A deadlock requires which of the following conditions (Coffman conditions)?
options: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait
questions.explanation: All four Coffman conditions must hold simultaneously for deadlock to occur.

questions.prompt: What is context switching?
options: Switching between user mode and kernel mode
Saving the state of one process/thread and loading another's
Moving data from disk to RAM
Changing the priority of a running process
questions.explanation: Context switching saves the current execution state and restores another's so the CPU can run a different task.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of kernel mode?
options: Run user applications with fewer permissions
Execute privileged operations like I/O and memory management
Compile source code into machine instructions
questions.explanation: Kernel mode allows the OS to perform protected hardware and system operations unsafe for user mode.

questions.prompt: How does paging differ from segmentation?
options: Paging uses fixed-size blocks; segmentation uses variable-size logical segments
Paging is only used for cache; segmentation is only for disk
Paging requires more programmer effort than segmentation
Segmentation eliminates the need for a page table
questions.explanation: Paging splits memory into equal pages; segmentation divides a program into logical units like code, stack, and heap.

questions.prompt: In Round Robin scheduling, what determines how long each process runs before being preempted?
questions.explanation: Each process gets a fixed time slice (quantum); when it expires, the CPU moves to the next ready process.

questions.prompt: What is the primary difference between a mutex and a semaphore?
options: A mutex allows multiple threads in; a semaphore allows only one
A mutex is typically binary (one owner); a semaphore can permit a counted number of concurrent accesses
A mutex is for processes only; a semaphore is for threads only
A mutex prevents deadlock; a semaphore causes deadlock
questions.explanation: Mutexes enforce mutual exclusion for one holder; counting semaphores can allow N simultaneous accesses.

questions.prompt: What is thrashing?
options: When the CPU runs at 100% utilization efficiently
When excessive paging causes the system to spend most time on disk I/O instead of useful work
When a thread exits before acquiring a lock
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when there is insufficient physical memory and constant page faults dominate performance.

questions.prompt: Why does a program use a system call?
options: To bypass the OS entirely for faster I/O
To request a privileged service from the operating system kernel
To allocate stack space for local variables
To convert high-level code to bytecode
questions.explanation: System calls are the controlled interface through which user programs ask the kernel to perform protected operations.

questions.prompt: The producer-consumer problem primarily illustrates the need for:
options: Synchronization between threads sharing a bounded buffer
questions.explanation: Producers and consumers must coordinate access to shared buffer space to avoid race conditions and overflow/underflow.

questions.prompt: Which SQL clause filters rows before grouping?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before aggregation; HAVING filters after GROUP BY.

questions.prompt: What property ensures a transaction is all-or-nothing?
questions.explanation: Atomicity guarantees that either all operations in a transaction commit or none do.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a database index?
options: To speed up data retrieval at the cost of extra storage and write overhead
questions.explanation: Indexes create lookup structures (like B-trees) that reduce query scan time.

questions.prompt: In a relational database, a foreign key is used to:
options: Uniquely identify each row in a table
Reference a primary key in another table to enforce relationships
Index a column for faster search
questions.explanation: Foreign keys link rows across tables and enforce referential integrity.

questions.prompt: Which normal form eliminates partial dependencies on a composite primary key?
questions.explanation: Second Normal Form (2NF) removes partial dependencies — non-key attributes must depend on the entire primary key.

questions.prompt: What does an INNER JOIN return?
options: All rows from both tables regardless of match
Only rows where the join condition matches in both tables
All rows from the left table and matching rows from the right
Only rows that appear in exactly one table
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN includes only rows with matching key values in both joined tables.

questions.prompt: Which isolation problem occurs when a transaction reads uncommitted data from another transaction?
questions.explanation: A dirty read sees data that may be rolled back if the other transaction aborts.

questions.prompt: How does a PRIMARY KEY differ from a UNIQUE constraint?
options: PRIMARY KEY allows NULL; UNIQUE does not
PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies a row and a table typically has one; UNIQUE allows one NULL (in SQL) and a table may have several
UNIQUE is faster than PRIMARY KEY for all queries
PRIMARY KEY automatically creates a foreign key
questions.explanation: Both enforce uniqueness, but PRIMARY KEY is the main row identifier and implies NOT NULL.

questions.prompt: What is the main goal of database normalization?
options: Reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity
Convert relational data to JSON documents
questions.explanation: Normalization organizes data to minimize duplication and update anomalies.

questions.prompt: In ACID, what does Durability guarantee?
options: Transactions execute in isolation from each other
All constraints are validated before commit
questions.explanation: Once a transaction commits, its effects persist even if the system crashes immediately after.

questions.prompt: What is the best defense against SQL injection in application code?
options: Building queries by concatenating user input
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries separate SQL structure from user data, preventing injected commands from executing.

questions.prompt: When is a NoSQL document store often a reasonable choice over a relational database?
options: When complex multi-table joins and strict ACID across entities are the primary need
When schema is flexible and data is naturally hierarchical or document-shaped
When every query requires strong relational normalization
When SQL is required by regulation in all cases
questions.explanation: Document stores fit evolving schemas and nested data; relational DBs excel at structured relationships and complex joins.

questions.prompt: What does a hash map store?
questions.explanation: A hash map associates each key with a value and uses the key's hash to find its bucket.

questions.prompt: In a binary tree, what is a *leaf* node?
options: A node with exactly one child
questions.explanation: A leaf has no children. The root is the only node with no parent.

questions.prompt: Which operation adds an element to the top of a stack?
questions.explanation: `push` adds to the top of a stack and `pop` removes from the top. `enqueue` is the queue equivalent.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from *n* unsorted elements with bottom-up heapify?
questions.explanation: Bottom-up heapify is O(n): most nodes sit near the bottom and sift down only a few levels, so the total work sums to a linear bound.

questions.prompt: Which structure gives O(1) average-time insert, delete, AND lookup by key?
questions.explanation: Hash tables give average O(1) for all three. A sorted array needs O(n) to insert, a linked list O(n) to look up, and a heap only finds the min/max fast.

questions.prompt: Why can an unbalanced binary search tree degrade to O(n) search?
options: Inserting sorted keys can make it a linked-list-shaped chain
Every node stores the whole subtree
questions.explanation: Inserting keys in sorted order puts each new key on the same side, so the tree's height becomes n. Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) keep the height O(log n).

questions.prompt: What is the amortized cost of `append` on a dynamic array that doubles its capacity when full?
questions.explanation: An occasional resize copies n elements, but doubling means resizes are rare. Spread over all appends, the cost is O(1) each.

questions.prompt: A trie is especially efficient for which task?
options: Finding the median of a stream
questions.explanation: A trie shares common prefixes, so finding all keys with a prefix costs O(length of prefix) plus the size of the output.

questions.prompt: Which pair of structures is the classic way to build an LRU cache with O(1) get and put?
options: A binary search tree and a queue
A hash map and a doubly linked list
questions.explanation: The hash map finds a node in O(1). The doubly linked list moves it to the front, or evicts the tail, in O(1).

questions.prompt: In a hash table using open addressing, what problem does a high load factor cause?
options: Long probe sequences, so slower operations
The table must become a tree
questions.explanation: As the table fills, colliding keys form clusters and probes get longer. Tables resize when the load factor passes a threshold, often about 0.7.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search?
questions.explanation: Linear search may have to check every element before finding the target, or before concluding it's absent.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm repeatedly swaps adjacent elements that are out of order?
questions.explanation: Bubble sort makes passes that swap adjacent out-of-order pairs, so the largest values 'bubble' to the end.

questions.prompt: What does Big-O notation describe?
options: The exact running time in seconds
The number of lines of code
An upper bound on how cost grows with input size
questions.explanation: Big-O gives an asymptotic upper bound on growth. It ignores constants and hardware.

questions.prompt: Which traversal goes as deep as possible along a branch before backtracking?
questions.explanation: DFS follows one path to its end, then backtracks. It's usually done with recursion or an explicit stack.

questions.prompt: What is *memoization*?
options: Storing the results of subproblems so they aren't recomputed
questions.explanation: Memoization caches function results by input. It's the top-down form of dynamic programming.

questions.prompt: Without memoization, what is the time complexity of naive recursive Fibonacci?
questions.explanation: Each call branches into two and recomputes the same subproblems, so the work grows exponentially. Memoization makes it O(n).

questions.prompt: Topological sort applies to which kind of graph?
questions.explanation: A topological order exists only if the directed graph has no cycles: each edge u→v needs u before v.

questions.prompt: Why can Dijkstra's algorithm give wrong answers with negative edge weights?
options: It runs in exponential time on them
It finalizes a vertex's distance early, assuming paths only get longer
questions.explanation: Dijkstra greedily settles the closest unsettled vertex. A later negative edge could make a shorter path to it. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights.

questions.prompt: What is the lower bound for comparison-based sorting in the worst case?
questions.explanation: A comparison sort must tell apart n! orderings, and a decision tree with n! leaves has height Ω(log n!) = Ω(n log n).

questions.prompt: The 0/1 knapsack DP over n items with capacity W runs in O(nW). Why is that called *pseudo-polynomial*?
options: W is a number, so the time is exponential in the bits needed to write W
It only works for small n
questions.explanation: The running time is polynomial in W's value but exponential in its bit length, which is the true input size.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of an operating system?
options: Manage hardware resources and give programs services
questions.explanation: The OS manages the CPU, memory, storage, and devices, and gives programs abstractions like processes and files.

questions.prompt: What is a *process*?
options: A program in execution, with its own address space
questions.explanation: A process is a running instance of a program: code plus its own memory, registers, and OS resources.

questions.prompt: Which memory is fastest for the CPU to access?
questions.explanation: Registers sit inside the CPU. Then come the caches (L1/L2/L3), then RAM, then storage.

questions.prompt: What is the role of a *device driver*?
options: Let the OS talk to a specific piece of hardware
questions.explanation: A driver translates generic OS requests into commands for one specific device.

questions.prompt: What is a *race condition*?
options: Two threads compete for the fastest CPU
The result depends on the unpredictable timing of concurrent accesses to shared data
A process using too much memory
questions.explanation: If unsynchronized threads read and write shared state, the result depends on how they interleave. Locks or atomics prevent it.

questions.prompt: What does a TLB (translation lookaside buffer) cache?
questions.explanation: The TLB caches page-table entries, so most address translations skip walking the page table in memory.

questions.prompt: What happens on a *page fault*?
options: The OS loads the missing page from disk (or reports an invalid access)
questions.explanation: The hardware traps to the OS, which loads the page and resumes the process. If the address was invalid, it raises an error such as a segfault.

questions.prompt: Always acquiring locks in one global order (*resource ordering*) prevents deadlock by breaking which Coffman condition?
questions.explanation: If every thread takes locks in the same global order, a cycle of threads waiting on each other can't form.

questions.prompt: What is *priority inversion*?
options: A high-priority task waits on a lock held by a low-priority task that is itself preempted by medium-priority tasks
The scheduler reverses all priorities each tick
A task lowers its own priority to save power
questions.explanation: Medium-priority work keeps the lock holder off the CPU, so the high-priority task stalls. Priority inheritance is the usual fix.

questions.prompt: Why does copy-on-write make `fork()` cheap?
options: It skips creating a new process
Parent and child share pages until one writes, and only then is that page copied
It copies memory to disk instead of RAM
It runs the child in kernel mode
questions.explanation: Pages start shared and read-only. A write triggers a fault that copies just that page, so pages that are never written are never copied.

questions.prompt: Which SQL statement reads data from a table?
questions.explanation: `SELECT` queries rows. INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE change data.

questions.prompt: What does `NULL` mean in SQL?
questions.explanation: NULL marks an unknown or missing value. Compare with `IS NULL`, because `= NULL` is never true.

questions.prompt: Which clause filters groups *after* aggregation?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before GROUP BY. HAVING filters the grouped results, e.g. `HAVING COUNT(*) > 5`.

questions.prompt: What does a LEFT JOIN return?
options: All rows from the left table, plus matching right rows (NULLs where there's no match)
Only matching rows from both tables
questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every left row. Right-side columns are NULL where nothing matches.

questions.prompt: What is a *composite* primary key?
options: A key made of two or more columns
A key stored in another table
A key with a UNIQUE index only
questions.explanation: A composite key uses the combination of several columns to identify a row, e.g. (student_id, course_id).

questions.prompt: Which isolation anomaly is a *non-repeatable read*?
options: Reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values
Two transactions both waiting on each other
Losing a committed write after a crash
questions.explanation: Another transaction committed an update between your two reads of the same row. REPEATABLE READ or higher prevents it.

questions.prompt: Why might adding many indexes to a table slow down the application?
options: Every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also update each index
questions.explanation: Indexes speed up reads, but each write has to maintain every index, which costs time and storage.

questions.prompt: What is a *phantom read*?
options: A re-run range query returns new rows inserted by another committed transaction
Reading a row deleted by a crash
questions.explanation: The rows matching a predicate changed between your two runs of the same query. SERIALIZABLE isolation prevents it.

questions.prompt: What does the CAP theorem say a distributed data store can't guarantee all at once during a network partition?
questions.explanation: During a partition, a system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a response).

questions.prompt: Why does a covering index speed up a query?
options: It caches the whole table in RAM
The index contains every column the query needs, so the base table isn't read
It removes the need for a WHERE clause
It sorts results by primary key
questions.explanation: When all the needed columns are in the index, the database answers from the index alone and skips the extra lookups into the table.
